vtrmc-1995-01.title: Split along the line $3x=2y$
vtrmc-1995-01.body:
In the rectangle $0\le x\le2$, $0\le y\le3$ the diagonal $3x=2y$ joins $(0,0)$ and $(2,3)$. Let
$$A=\{3x\le2y\}=\{0\le y\le3,\ 0\le x\le\tfrac{2y}3\},\qquad B=\{3x\ge2y\}=\{0\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le\tfrac{3x}2\}.$$
On $A$ the maximum is $2y$, on $B$ it is $3x$. Hence
$$I=\int_0^3\!\!\int_0^{2y/3}\frac{dx\,dy}{1+4y^2}+\int_0^2\!\!\int_0^{3x/2}\frac{dy\,dx}{1+9x^2}=\int_0^3\frac{2y/3}{1+4y^2}\,dy+\int_0^2\frac{3x/2}{1+9x^2}\,dx .$$
Both are logarithmic integrals:
$$\int_0^3\frac{2y/3}{1+4y^2}\,dy=\Bigl[\tfrac1{12}\ln(1+4y^2)\Bigr]_0^3=\frac{\ln37}{12},\qquad\int_0^2\frac{3x/2}{1+9x^2}\,dx=\Bigl[\tfrac1{12}\ln(1+9x^2)\Bigr]_0^2=\frac{\ln37}{12}.$$
So $I=\dfrac{\ln37}{6}\approx0.60182$ (numerical integration gives the same value).

*Remark.* The official solution evaluates $\iint\frac{dx\,dy}{(1+\max(3x,2y))^2}$ instead, i.e. it reads the denominator as $(1+\max)^2$, and obtains $\frac{7\ln7-6}{21}$. The integral as printed, with $1+(\max)^2$, equals $\frac{\ln 37}{6}$.

**Answer:** $\frac{\ln37}{6}$.

vtrmc-1995-01.title: Rescale to a square
vtrmc-1995-01.body:
Substitute $u=3x$, $v=2y$, so $dx\,dy=\frac16\,du\,dv$ and the rectangle becomes the square $[0,6]^2$:
$$I=\frac16\iint_{[0,6]^2}\frac{du\,dv}{1+\max(u,v)^2}.$$
The set of points of the square with $\max(u,v)\le s$ is $[0,s]^2$, of area $s^2$, so the "layer" where $\max(u,v)\in[s,s+ds]$ has area $2s\,ds$. Therefore
$$I=\frac16\int_0^6\frac{2s}{1+s^2}\,ds=\frac16\ln37 .$$

**Answer:** $\frac{\ln37}{6}$.

vtrmc-1995-02.title: Matrix powers
vtrmc-1995-02.body:
Write $\theta(\mathbf v)=A\mathbf v+\mathbf u$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}4&-3\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf u=\binom11$. By induction,
$$\theta^{100}(\mathbf v)=A^{100}\mathbf v+\bigl(A^{99}+A^{98}+\dots+A+I\bigr)\mathbf u .$$
The characteristic polynomial is $(x-4)(x+1)+6=x^2-3x+2=(x-1)(x-2)$. An eigenvector for $1$ is $\mathbf u=\binom11$ (indeed $A\mathbf u=\binom11$), and one for $2$ is $\binom32$.

- Since $A\mathbf u=\mathbf u$, $\bigl(A^{99}+\dots+I\bigr)\mathbf u=100\,\mathbf u=\binom{100}{100}$.
- Write $\mathbf v=\binom10=-2\binom11+\binom32$. Then $A^{100}\mathbf v=-2\binom11+2^{100}\binom32$.

Adding, $\theta^{100}(1,0)=\bigl(-2+3\cdot2^{100}+100,\ -2+2\cdot2^{100}+100\bigr)=\bigl(98+3\cdot2^{100},\ 98+2\cdot2^{100}\bigr)$.

(Iterating $\theta$ $100$ times with exact integer arithmetic gives the same pair.)

vtrmc-1995-02.title: Find quantities that behave simply
vtrmc-1995-02.body:
Look for linear combinations of the coordinates that transform simply under $\theta$. If $(x',y')=\theta(x,y)$:
- $x'-y'=(4x-3y+1)-(2x-y+1)=2(x-y)$, so $x-y$ doubles at each step;
- $2x'-3y'=2(4x-3y+1)-3(2x-y+1)=2x-3y-1$, so $2x-3y$ decreases by $1$ at each step.

Starting from $(1,0)$, where $x-y=1$ and $2x-3y=2$, after $100$ steps
$$x-y=2^{100},\qquad 2x-3y=2-100=-98 .$$
Substitute $x=y+2^{100}$ into $2x-3y=-98$ to get $-y+2^{101}=-98$, so $y=98+2^{101}=98+2\cdot2^{100}$ and $x=98+3\cdot2^{100}$.

**Answer:** $\theta^{100}(1,0)=(98+3\cdot2^{100},\ 98+2\cdot2^{100})$.

vtrmc-1995-03.title: Work modulo $x^{n+1}$
vtrmc-1995-03.body:
Let $s=x+x^2+\dots+x^n$, so $f=\sum_{k=0}^n(-s)^k$. By the finite geometric sum,
$$f\cdot(1+s)=1-(-s)^{n+1}=1+(-1)^ns^{n+1}.$$
Every term of $s^{n+1}$ has degree at least $n+1$, so $f(1+s)\equiv1\pmod{x^{n+1}}$ (congruence of polynomials: the difference is divisible by $x^{n+1}$).

Also $(1-x)(1+s)=(1-x)(1+x+\dots+x^n)=1-x^{n+1}\equiv1\pmod{x^{n+1}}$. Multiply the first congruence by $1-x$:
$$f\equiv f\cdot(1+s)(1-x)\equiv1-x\pmod{x^{n+1}}.$$
So $f(x)=1-x+(\text{terms of degree}\ge n+1)$, and the coefficient of $x^r$ is $0$ for $2\le r\le n$. ∎

(For example, for $n=3$ one gets $f=1-x-4x^5+\dots$; a computer expansion for $n=2,\dots,7$ confirms the zero coefficients.)

vtrmc-1995-03.title: Power series (official idea)
vtrmc-1995-03.body:
Consider the formal power series $g(x)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k(x+\dots+x^n)^k$. The terms with $k\ge n+1$ only contain powers $x^m$ with $m\ge k\ge n+1$, so for $r\le n$ the coefficient of $x^r$ in $f$ equals that in $g$. Since $x+\dots+x^n=\frac{x(1-x^n)}{1-x}$ has zero constant term, $g$ is a geometric series with ratio $-\frac{x(1-x^n)}{1-x}$:
$$g(x)=\frac{1}{1+\frac{x(1-x^n)}{1-x}}=\frac{1-x}{1-x^{n+1}}=(1-x)\bigl(1+x^{n+1}+x^{2n+2}+\cdots\bigr).$$
The coefficients of $x^2,\dots,x^n$ here are $0$. ∎

vtrmc-1995-04.title: Use $\tau^2=\tau+1$ and $1/\tau=\tau-1$
vtrmc-1995-04.body:
Recall $\tau^2=\tau+1$, so $\frac1\tau=\tau-1$, and $1<\tau<2$; $\tau$ is irrational.

Let $p=[\tau n]$, a positive integer (as $\tau n>1$). Since $\tau n$ is irrational, $p<\tau n<p+1$. Dividing by $\tau$ and using $\frac1\tau=\tau-1$:
$$p(\tau-1)<n<(p+1)(\tau-1),$$
i.e.
$$p\tau-p<n<p\tau-p+\tau-1 .$$
The left inequality gives $p\tau<n+p$. The right one gives $p\tau>n+p+1-\tau>n+p-1$ (as $\tau<2$). Thus $n+p-1<p\tau<n+p$, and therefore
$$n+p<\tau p+1<n+p+1,\qquad\text{so}\qquad[\tau[\tau n]+1]=[\tau p+1]=n+p .$$
On the other hand $\tau^2n=\tau n+n$, and $p<\tau n<p+1$ gives $[\tau^2n]=p+n$. The two sides agree. ∎

(A direct check for $n=1,\dots,300$ with exact arithmetic confirms the identity.)

vtrmc-1995-05.title: Iterate the inequality along a chain
vtrmc-1995-05.body:
**Key estimate.** Let $y<z$ and let $n\ge1$. Choose points $z=p_1>p_2>\dots>p_n=y$ (possible for every $n$). Since $t\mapsto t^3$ is increasing on $\mathbb R$, the inequalities $\theta(p_{i+1})<\theta(p_i)^3$ can be chained:
$$\theta(y)<\theta(p_{n-1})^3<\theta(p_{n-2})^{9}<\dots<\theta(z)^{3^{n-1}}. \tag{$*$}$$

**Part 1: $\theta(x)>-1$.** Suppose $\theta(x)\le-1$ for some $x$. Fix any $y<x$ and let $z=\frac{x+y}2$. Then $\theta(z)<\theta(x)^3\le-1$. By $(*)$, for every $n$,
$$\theta(y)<\theta(z)^{3^{n-1}}=-|\theta(z)|^{3^{n-1}}\longrightarrow-\infty\quad(n\to\infty),$$
because $|\theta(z)|>1$ and $3^{n-1}$ is odd. This is impossible for the fixed real number $\theta(y)$. Hence $\theta(x)>-1$ for all $x$.

**Part 2.** First a lemma: *if $a<b$ and $\theta(a),\theta(b)\in[0,1]$, then $\theta(a)=0$.* For $c\in(a,b)$ we have $\theta(c)^3>\theta(a)\ge0$, so $\theta(c)>0$, and $\theta(c)<\theta(b)^3\le1$; thus $0<\theta(c)<1$ on $(a,b)$. Apply $(*)$ with $y=a$ and $z=\frac{a+b}2$: $\theta(a)<\theta(z)^{3^{n-1}}\to0$, so $\theta(a)\le0$, i.e. $\theta(a)=0$.

Now suppose $a<b$ both have $\theta\in[0,1]$. Let $c=\frac{a+b}{2}$; as shown, $0<\theta(c)<1$. Then $c<b$ with $\theta(c),\theta(b)\in[0,1]$, so by the lemma $\theta(c)=0$, a contradiction. Hence $0\le\theta(x)\le1$ for at most one $x$. ∎

vtrmc-1995-06.title: The astroid in each corner
vtrmc-1995-06.body:
**Where can the rod be?** The two ends are $4$ inches apart. They cannot be on opposite sides ($12$ inches apart). If they are on the same side, the rod lies along that side and paints no area. Otherwise the ends are on two adjacent sides, within $4$ inches of the common corner; as $4<6$, the four corner regions do not overlap. So the answer is $4$ times the area $A$ painted near one corner.

**One corner.** Put the corner at the origin with the sides along the positive axes. The rod joins $(4\cos t,0)$ and $(0,4\sin t)$, $0\le t\le\frac\pi2$; for $0<t<\frac\pi2$ its points $(x,y)$ satisfy $x,y\ge0$ and
$$\frac{x}{\cos t}+\frac{y}{\sin t}=4 .$$
Fix $(x,y)$ with $x,y>0$ and let $\varphi(t)=\frac{x}{\cos t}+\frac{y}{\sin t}$ on $(0,\frac\pi2)$. It is continuous and tends to $+\infty$ at both ends, so $(x,y)$ is painted iff $\min\varphi\le4$. From $\varphi'(t)=\frac{x\sin t}{\cos^2t}-\frac{y\cos t}{\sin^2t}=0$ we get $\tan^3t=\frac yx$, and there
$$\cos t=\frac{x^{1/3}}{\sqrt{x^{2/3}+y^{2/3}}},\quad\sin t=\frac{y^{1/3}}{\sqrt{x^{2/3}+y^{2/3}}},\quad\min\varphi=\bigl(x^{2/3}+y^{2/3}\bigr)^{3/2}.$$
So the painted region is $\{x,y\ge0:\ x^{2/3}+y^{2/3}\le4^{2/3}\}$, bounded by the astroid $x=4\cos^3u$, $y=4\sin^3u$.

**Its area.**
$$A=\int_0^{\pi/2}y\,\Bigl|\frac{dx}{du}\Bigr|\,du=\int_0^{\pi/2}4\sin^3u\cdot12\cos^2u\sin u\,du=48\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^4u\cos^2u\,du .$$
Since $\sin^4u\cos^2u=\frac{\sin^22u}{4}\cdot\frac{1-\cos2u}{2}$, and $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^22u\,du=\frac\pi4$, $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^22u\cos2u\,du=0$, the integral is $\frac{\pi}{32}$ and $A=\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

**Total:** $4\cdot\frac{3\pi}2=6\pi\approx18.85$ square inches.

vtrmc-1995-06.title: Maximise the height for fixed $x$ (official approach)
vtrmc-1995-06.body:
With the corner at the origin, the rod from $(a,0)$ to $(0,\sqrt{16-a^2})$ is the line $y=\left(1-\frac xa\right)\sqrt{16-a^2}$, $0\le x\le a$. For fixed $x\in[0,4]$, the heights reached as $a$ runs from $x$ to $4$ fill an interval from $0$ to the maximum (by continuity), so the painted area is $\int_0^4y_{\max}(x)\,dx$.

Setting $\frac{\partial y}{\partial a}=\frac{x}{a^2}\sqrt{16-a^2}-\left(1-\frac xa\right)\frac{a}{\sqrt{16-a^2}}=0$ and multiplying by $a^2\sqrt{16-a^2}$ gives $x(16-a^2)=a^3-xa^2$, i.e. $a^3=16x$. Use $a$ as the integration variable: $x=\frac{a^3}{16}$, $dx=\frac{3a^2}{16}da$, and $y_{\max}=\left(1-\frac{a^2}{16}\right)\sqrt{16-a^2}=\frac{(16-a^2)^{3/2}}{16}$:
$$A=\int_0^4\frac{(16-a^2)^{3/2}}{16}\cdot\frac{3a^2}{16}\,da .$$
With $a=4\sin t$: $A=\int_0^{\pi/2}48\cos^4t\sin^2t\,dt=\int_0^{\pi/2}6\sin^22t\,(1+\cos2t)\,dt=\frac{3\pi}{2}$. Four corners give $6\pi$.

**Answer:** $6\pi$ square inches.

vtrmc-1995-07.title: $f$ is the sum of prime factors
vtrmc-1995-07.body:
$f(n)$ is the sum of the prime factors of $n$ counted with multiplicity; hence $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$.

**Lemma 1.** For integers $a,b\ge2$, $a+b\le ab$, with equality only for $a=b=2$ (because $ab-a-b=(a-1)(b-1)-1$). Consequently, if $n$ has prime factors $q_1,\dots,q_m$ (with multiplicity), then $f(n)=q_1+\dots+q_m\le q_1\cdots q_m=n$, with equality iff $n$ is prime or $n=4$. (Induct on $m$: $q_1+\dots+q_m\le q_1\cdots q_{m-1}+q_m\le q_1\cdots q_m$; for $m\ge3$ the first factor is $\ge4$, so the last step is strict.)

**$g$ is well defined.** By Lemma 1 the sequence $n,f(n),f^2(n),\dots$ is a non-increasing sequence of integers $\ge2$, so it is eventually constant; its final value $g(n)$ is a fixed point of $f$, i.e. a prime or $4$. Also $g(n)\le f(n)$.

**(i)** $100=2^2\cdot5^2$: $f(100)=4+10=14$, $f(14)=2+7=9$, $f(9)=3+3=6$, $f(6)=2+3=5$, and $5$ is fixed. So $g(100)=5$. Next $f(10^{10})=f(2^{10}5^{10})=20+50=70$, $f(70)=2+5+7=14$, and then as before $14\to9\to6\to5$. So $g(10^{10})=5$.

*(The official solution stops at $6$ and states $g(100)=g(10^{10})=6$; but $f(6)=5$, so the limit is $5$.)*

**(ii)** Let $n>1$ be odd.
- If $n$ is prime, $g(n)=n$, so $n$ does not have property H.
- **Lemma 2.** If $n$ is odd and composite and $n\ne9,15$, then $f(n)\le n/2$. Write $n=q_1\cdots q_m$ with odd primes $q_1\le\dots\le q_m$, $m\ge2$. For $m=2$: $a+b\le\frac{ab}2\iff(a-2)(b-2)\ge4$; with $3\le a\le b$ odd primes this fails only for $a=3$, $b\in\{3,5\}$, i.e. $n\in\{9,15\}$. For $m\ge3$: let $P=q_1\cdots q_{m-1}\ge9$ and $q=q_m\ge3$; by Lemma 1, $f(n)=f(P)+q\le P+q$, and $P+q\le\frac{Pq}{2}\iff(P-2)(q-2)\ge4$, true since $(P-2)(q-2)\ge7$.

  For such $n$, $g(n)\le f(n)\le n/2$, so $n$ does not have property H.
- $n=9$: $9\to6\to5$, so $g(9)=5$ and $4.5<5<9$. **Property H holds.**
- $n=15$: $15\to8\to6\to5$, so $g(15)=5<7.5$. Property H fails.

Hence the only odd integer $n>1$ with property H is $9$. (A computer check of all odd $n<20000$ finds only $n=9$.)

**Answer:** (i) $g(100)=5$, $g(10^{10})=5$; (ii) $n=9$ only. ∎
